newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian Metals - Copper rally seen losing steam.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - Copper rally seen losing steam.

text.p: A modest rally in copper prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) may short itself out because it is led by speculative buying and interest remains weak, metal traders said on Friday.
"I don't think it can continue and it will come down again," Vinod Kumar, director of Singapore-based metal company Donald Mcarthy, told Reuters.
"There's not much interest at all. Volume on the LME is quite low," a dealer with a Western metal trading company said.
Kumar said the recent rise in three-month copper prices on the LME, which began on Tuesday, was fuelled mainly by speculative buying.
"China is quiet. Domestic prices are high, so they're not exporting any stuff out," the managing director of a Japanese metal trading firm said.
Copper prices ended the kerb on Thursday at $1,936 a tonne, up $11 from Wednesday, down from an intra-day peak of $1,953.
Three-month prices in the Far East were quoted slightly up at around $1,940/46 a tonne at 0300 GMT on Friday.
Over the next week, traders said they expected copper prices to fluctuate between $1,900-$1,950 a tonne and trade to remain thin.
"It's going to be probably quiet after the Sumitomo announcement," one dealer said. "It may be hard to sustain a move up towards $2,000."

Japanese giant Sumitomo Corp raised on Thursday its estimate of the losses on illicit copper deals by dismissed star trader Yasuo Hamanaka from $1.8 billion to $2.6 billion and said it would seek the prosecution of the one-time copper king.
The announcement was greeted with yawns by traders in Singapore.

"The market has put the Sumitomo affair behind it," a Japanese trader said. "It really has no impact anymore, although there may still be some questions about his actions and the liquidation of Sumitomo's positions."
"People were expecting $5.0 billion in losses and when they came back and said $2.6 billion, people were happy," Kumar said.
Another trader said the announcement would shore up somewhat the still shaky confidence of punters in the market.
"This will give people some confidence that there will be no more heavy selling in the market over the short-term," the trader said.
Sumitomo's initial announcement last June rocked the base metal market and sent copper tumbling sharply to a two-year low below $1,800 a tonne.
The only bright spot in a drab Asian base metals market now is steady aluminium demand in Japan and spot inquiries from China, traders said.
Firm demand has led to the diversion of Russian aluminium, which used to wind up in Singapore, to the Japanese market, driving premiums in the city-state up, dealers said.

"Most of the stuff is going to Japan. Aluminium premiums are increasing because the Russian material here is very small," a Japanese trader said, adding demand should reach over 50,000 tonnes until the year-end.
Aluminium premiums have gone up to around $50-$75 a tonne from last week's level of $40-$60, traders said.
